source.author: lucan
source.text: Sed mihi nec motus nemorum, nec litoris ictus, Nec placet incertus, qui provocat aequora, Delphin: Aut siccum quod mergus amat: quodque ausa volare Ardea sublimis pennae confisa natanti: Quodque caput spargens undis, velut occupet imbrem, Instabili gressu metitur litora cornix.
source.text_original: Sed mihi nec motus nemorum, nec litoris ictus, / Nec placet incertus, qui provocat aequora, Delphin: / Aut siccum quod mergus amat: quodque ausa volare / Ardea sublimis pennae confisa natanti: / Quodque caput spargens undis, velut occupet imbrem, / Instabili gressu metitur litora cornix.
source.text_english: But I do not care for the movements of the groves, nor the beating of the shore, nor the uncertain dolphin that challenges the waters; nor the dry land that the mergus loves; nor the Ardea, bold in flight and trusting her swimming wings; nor the crow, splashing its head with waves, as though to seize the rain, and treading the shore with unsteady step.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: Tyrrheni tergore piscis Peleos in thalamos vehitur Thetis; aequora delphin corripit, illa sedet deiecta in lumina palla nec love maiorem nasci suspirat Achillen.
reuse.text_original: Tyrrheni tergore piscis / Peleos in thalamos vehitur Thetis; aequora delphin / corripit, illa sedet deiecta in lumina palla / nec love maiorem nasci suspirat Achillen.
reuse.text_english: Peleus is borne to the bridal chambers by Thetis, a Tyrrhenian fish, on its back; the dolphin speeds over the seas. She sits with her cloak fallen over her eyes and does not sigh that Achilles is born, greater than Jupiter.
